artifacts.caption: Harrison H4 marine chronometer — portable time precise enough for longitude at sea.
artifacts.description: Harrison's chronometer on display at National Maritime Museum in Greenwich

artifacts.file: Lever of a Watch Lever Escapement.jpg
artifacts.caption: Swiss lever escapement — the fork that releases the train in equal ticks.
artifacts.description: Pallet fork or Pallet lever of a Watch Lever escapement
artifacts.commons_file: Lever of a Watch Lever Escapement.jpg

artifacts.caption: Lever escapement diagram — pallets, escape wheel, and the path of each tick.

artifacts.caption: Balance wheel and hairspring — the oscillator that “keeps” the time.
artifacts.description: A bimetallic temperature compensated balance wheel from an early 1900s pocket watch.  1.8cm diameter.  The rim is made of two bimetallic semicircular arms, composed of a layer of brass on the outside fused to a layer of steel on the inside.

artifacts.caption: Escapement with jewel bearings — rubies at the pivots that take the wear.
artifacts.description: The balance wheel, pallet fork, escapement wheel, and a few of the gears of a Chinese TY2807 movement in a skeleton watch, as seen in File:Automatic skeleton watch.jpg.

artifacts.caption: Omega calibre 321 chronograph — column wheel and vertical clutch in the open.
artifacts.description:
Omega 17 jewel hand-wind column wheel screwed balance chronograph movement with 30-minute and 12-hour registers. Watch is a Omega Speedmaster 145.012 from 1967 with a Thomas Preik exhibition caseback.
